description: This course surveys the geographic patterns of economic activity, with a focus on cities. It examines issues related to history, efficiency, and governance. The course introduces and applies several economic frameworks, including gains from specialization and trade, location theory, central place theory, migration, real estate valuation, rent analysis, income--expenditure models, consumer and producer choice, and public choice.These perspectives will be applied to several important questions: Why do cities develop and grow? What makes them so prosperous? How and why do cities differ? What economic problems commonly arise in them? How can local governments work to solve those problems? How might state and federal programs complicate matters? Will cities continue to promise growth and prosperity in the future? Adding the human dimension and real-world complexity to economic theory, we will also explore urban issues through an applied project. Groups of three to five students will select a city of their choice and investigate a specific urban issue, examining local problems, services, and ventures and report their findings. Prerequisite: ECON 121 or permission of instructor.
